plain_summary: This lab studies how the three-dimensional folding of the genome inside the cell nucleus controls which genes get turned on or off. DNA doesn't sit in a straight line inside cells; it loops and folds so that distant regions can physically touch and influence each other. The lab uses techniques like Hi-C (which maps which parts of the genome touch), ChIP-seq, and single-cell RNA sequencing, often paired with computational tools they build themselves, to study this 3D genome architecture across diverse settings: immune cell development, brain and breast cancer, drug resistance, and even the malaria parasite. Understanding these folding patterns helps explain how cells become specialized, how tumors evade treatment, and how disease-related genes get switched on, pointing toward new therapeutic targets across cancer, immunology, and infectious disease.
trajectory: Recent work is moving from simply mapping 3D genome structure toward using it to identify functional, disease-driving genes — finding tumor-dependency genes in ependymoma and mechanisms of chemotherapy resistance in breast cancer via chromatin rewiring. In parallel, the lab is building computational tools (e.g., MuDCoD) to extract personalized, time-resolved network information from single-cell data, and extending 3D genome analysis to non-cancer systems such as malaria parasite virulence gene regulation and immune cell lineage commitment. The trajectory points toward translating chromatin architecture findings into therapeutic target identification across cancer and inflammatory disease.
